title: Cheese Soufflé
subtitle: Classic French risen cheese soufflé
excerpt: A twice-risen cheese soufflé with a rich, savoury béchamel base and stiffly beaten egg whites. Lighter than air, deeply flavoured, and not nearly as difficult as its reputation suggests.

recipe.sourceNotes: The soufflé is one of the most technically demanding of classic French dishes, and one of the most misunderstood. The word comes from the French souffler (to blow), and the dish dates from at least the early nineteenth century, when French chefs including Antonin Carême refined the technique of using stiffly beaten egg whites as a leavening agent in both sweet and savoury preparations. The soufflé's reputation for difficulty stems from the time between oven and table: once risen, it deflates within minutes. The twice-risen technique (making the base and folding in the whites, then baking just before serving) removes most of the timing difficulty and is used by professional kitchens. A soufflé made correctly from a properly seasoned, intensely flavoured base with correctly beaten whites will rise reliably every time.

recipeTools.notes: Four 200 ml individual soufflé dishes (ramekins), or one 1.2-litre soufflé dish.

content.text: The most common soufflé failures are under-seasoning the base (the whites dilute the flavour, so the base must taste slightly too strong) and over- or under-beating the whites. Beat to firm peaks that just hold their shape but are not dry and grainy. Fold gently: a few streaks of white are better than a deflated mixture. Butter and coat the dishes with Parmesan before filling: this creates a surface the soufflé can grip as it rises.

items.preparation: finely grated; 20 g for the batter, 20 g to coat the dishes

content.text: Butter 4 individual ramekins generously and coat the inside with grated Parmesan by rotating and tapping. Place in the fridge. Heat the oven to 200 C / fan 180 C / gas 6.

Make the béchamel: melt the butter in a saucepan, stir in the flour, cook for 2 minutes. Gradually whisk in the milk. Cook for 5 minutes until very thick. Remove from the heat and stir in the Cheddar, 20 g Parmesan, mustard, cayenne, nutmeg, and salt. Beat in the 4 egg yolks. The base should taste slightly overseasoned.

Whisk the 5 egg whites with a pinch of salt to firm peaks. Stir a large spoonful into the cheese mixture to loosen it. Gently fold in the remaining whites in two batches, preserving as much volume as possible.

Divide the mixture between the prepared ramekins, filling to within 1 cm of the rim. Run your thumb around the inside edge to create a shallow groove (this helps the soufflé rise straight). Bake for 12 to 14 minutes until well risen and golden on top but still with a slight wobble. Serve immediately.
